name: Pesto Pasta
steps: Check the fusilli is eggless and the hard cheese is explicitly made with vegetarian coagulants; traditional Parmesan is not suitable. Pick and wash the basil leaves, then dry them completely so the pesto does not turn watery. Peel and roughly chop garlic. Set aside a few small basil leaves for finishing.

Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan over low-medium heat for 2–3 minutes, shaking often, until lightly golden, not dark. Cool, then reserve 15 g for garnish. Finely grate the cheese and reserve 10 g for garnish. Put the remaining 55 g nuts, 60 g cheese, garlic and 4 g salt into a processor and pulse to coarse crumbs.

Add most of the basil and pulse briefly, scraping the sides. Stream in the olive oil and lemon juice while pulsing just until a textured green sauce forms. Avoid a long continuous blend, which heats and darkens the basil. Keep the pesto at room temperature while the pasta cooks.

Bring 2500 ml water and the remaining 8 g salt to a rolling boil. Add fusilli and cook to the packet's al dente time, stirring at the start. Before draining, scoop out about 80 ml of the starchy pasta water. Drain the pasta well without rinsing.

Put the hot fusilli in a large warm bowl off the heat. Add pesto and toss gently, adding the reserved pasta water a little at a time until the sauce coats the twists without pooling. Divide into four bowls and top with reserved pine nuts, cheese and basil leaves. Serve immediately; do not boil the pesto after mixing.
tips: Pine nuts are a major allergen. This fresh basil pesto uses vegetarian hard cheese in place of animal-rennet Parmesan. A splash of starchy pasta water makes the pesto cling without cream; keep the finished sauce off direct heat to preserve its green color.
notes: Quantities serve four adults. Check the doneness cues in each step and adjust seasoning to taste. Jain suitability depends on your household ingredient rules.
